h1:
Banana Chips & Dried Banana
Where to Buy Nakhon Nayok Souvenirs
intro: Nakhon Nayok has always been banana country. When the nam wa bananas come in thick, locals turn the surplus into crispy banana chips, chewy sun-dried bananas and sweet butter-baked bananas — the kind of snack everyone driving through ends up grabbing a bag of. This guide rounds up the shops actually open and selling right now, rough prices, and how to pick a bag that's crisp and fresh rather than gone soft from the humidity.

blocks.html: If you drive out from Bangkok to see the waterfalls or go rafting in Nakhon Nayok, almost everyone heads home with a bag of banana chips riding along. This area grows a lot of nam wa bananas, and when the harvest is heavy people turn it into dried snacks that keep for a long time. The chips are sliced thin and fried crisp like potato crisps, the sun-dried bananas are dried in the sun until chewy and naturally sweet, and the butter-baked ones are sweeter and richer, easy to keep snacking on. Here's where to buy, how to choose, and which shops people actually stop at.

blocks.text: The kinds of banana snacks you'll find in Nakhon Nayok

blocks.html: Before you go shopping, it helps to know the different types, because a lot of shops sell them all mixed together — banana, taro, sweet potato and pumpkin.

items: Banana chips (kluai chap) — green nam wa bananas sliced thin and fried crisp, in sweet sugar-glazed, salted and paprika flavours. This is the local souvenir star.
Sun-dried banana (kluai tak) — ripe nam wa bananas dried in the sun until chewy and naturally sweet; some makers press them flat and glaze them with honey for shine.
Butter-baked banana — banana chips tossed with butter and sugar for a rich, buttery sweetness. Kids love it, and it's more moreish than the plain crisp version.
Taro, sweet potato and pumpkin chips — usually sold right beside the banana chips in the same shop, so you can mix a bag for anyone who doesn't fancy banana.

blocks.title: How to pick a bag that's actually crisp
blocks.html: Pick up a bag and give it a gentle shake — if it's crisp you'll hear a clear, sharp rattle; if it's quiet and soft, it's already gone a bit damp. Check the frying or production date on the bag too. Chips fried fresh that week are crisper than stock that's been sitting around.

blocks.text: Nakhon Nayok souvenir shops people actually stop at

blocks.html: Nakhon Nayok doesn't have big malls, so souvenirs are spread across roadside shops on the main routes and a handful of gift centres. We've ordered them by how convenient they are for anyone driving through, starting with the one place that has everything, down to the specialist shops that fry fresh.

items.name: Saranrom Nakhon Nayok Souvenirs
items.blurb: The most complete souvenir centre in town, with hundreds of OTOP products under one roof — banana chips, dried banana, taro chips, all the way to Ban Na chive cakes, tan palm cake and marian-plum rice crackers. There's a food court and coffee corner to take a break, and plenty of parking that can handle tour groups. Good if you want to make one stop and tick everything off.
items.meta: Rangsit–Nakhon Nayok Rd (4 km from Sam Sao junction) · open daily 08:00–19:00

items.name: Mae Tip Banana Chips (Sahathai Tha Thong Mai)
items.blurb: A banana-chip specialist that fries fresh every day. The whole point here is crisp, fresh and tight control over the ingredients — quality bananas, sliced evenly and thin. If you want chips that are genuinely crisp and not sitting in old stock, this is the one locals point you to. Find it around the Sahathai supermarket in Tha Thong Mai.
items.meta: Tha Thong Mai area, Mueang Nakhon Nayok

items.name: Khun Ae Chive Cakes & Phichaphat Souvenirs
items.blurb: A souvenir shop best known for thin-skinned Ban Na chive cakes, but you can grab banana chips and other dried snacks here too. Good if you want both a hot snack to eat now and keep-for-later souvenirs from a single shop.
items.meta: Mueang Nakhon Nayok (check opening hours on their page before going)
items.price: banana chips from a few tens of baht

items.name: Roadside stalls along Suwannason Road
items.blurb: All along Suwannason Road heading into town and out towards the waterfalls, roadside stalls sell banana chips, dried banana and taro chips, bundled into small bags at easy prices you can haggle over. The upside is they're easy to pull over at; the thing to watch is freshness, since some stalls leave the stock out in the sun for a long time.
items.meta: Along Suwannason Rd, town entrance to waterfall road

items.name: OTOP homemaker stalls, Ban Na–Pak Phli
items.blurb: Ban Na and Pak Phli districts have homemaker groups making dried banana and banana paste as community products — handmade, in small batches, but with a natural taste that isn't too sweet. If you pass an OTOP fair or a community market around there, keep an eye out.
items.meta: Ban Na / Pak Phli districts (at markets and OTOP fairs)

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Nakhon Nayok isn't a town with big-brand dried-banana makers like Bang Krathum in Phitsanulok. What it's genuinely known for is banana chips and marian-plum souvenirs. If you're really set on dried banana, look for the homemaker stalls or ask at Saranrom — you'll get more of the real local thing than from the generic roadside stalls.

blocks.text: Pair it with the town's other souvenirs

blocks.html: Since you're stopping at a souvenir shop anyway, a lot of people carry banana chips home alongside the other things Nakhon Nayok is known for, so you've got both snacks and proper food covered.

items.name: Marian plum & sweet plum-mango
items.blurb: The fruit Nakhon Nayok is most famous for — sweet with a hint of sour. You'll find it fresh from around February to April, and processed into rice crackers and candied versions sold all year.

items.name: Ban Na chive cakes
items.blurb: Thin-skinned chive cakes with a generous filling — the town's go-to snack. Eat them hot or carry them home; almost every souvenir shop sells them.

items.name: Tan palm cake & pandan layer cake
items.blurb: Fragrant Thai cakes that Saranrom smokes with scented candle. Good to bring back for older relatives alongside the banana chips.

blocks.text: How to store and carry them home without spoiling

items: Banana chips keep in a tightly sealed bag with the air pressed out, stored somewhere dry and out of the sun — they'll last several weeks. If they start going stale, a short blast in the microwave brings the crispness back.
Sun-dried banana has higher moisture, so keeping it in the regular fridge compartment makes it last longer and stops mould. If you buy the honey-glazed kind, watch out for it sticking together.
When transporting, keep the bags in a cool spot in the car — don't leave them sitting in a hot car in the sun, or the sugar glaze melts and goes sticky and the chips turn soft.
If you buy from several shops, separate the bags by production date and eat the older-fried ones first, saving the freshest for last.

faq.q: Where's the best place to buy Nakhon Nayok banana chips and dried banana?
faq.a: If you want everything in one stop, Saranrom Nakhon Nayok Souvenirs on Rangsit–Nakhon Nayok Road is the pick — open daily 08:00–19:00 with banana chips, dried banana, taro chips and hundreds of other souvenirs. If you specifically want banana chips fried fresh, try Mae Tip Banana Chips near Sahathai in Tha Thong Mai.

faq.q: Roughly how much do Nakhon Nayok banana chips cost?
faq.a: Small bags at roadside stalls start around ฿20–40, while standard bags at souvenir shops run about ฿35–60 depending on size and flavour. Homemaker-group dried banana packs are around ฿40–80.

faq.q: What's the difference between banana chips and butter-baked banana?
faq.a: Banana chips are thin-sliced bananas fried crisp, in sweet or salted flavours. Butter-baked banana takes those chips and tosses them with butter and sugar for a rich, buttery sweetness and a softer-crisp texture. Kids usually prefer the butter-baked kind.

faq.q: Does Nakhon Nayok have Phitsanulok-style dried banana?
faq.a: It does, but it isn't the town's signature the way it is in Phitsanulok. Most Nakhon Nayok dried banana comes from Ban Na–Pak Phli homemaker groups selling it as a community product. The town's real specialties are banana chips and marian-plum souvenirs.

faq.q: How long do banana chips keep?
faq.a: Sealed tightly and stored somewhere dry and out of the sun, they last several weeks to about a month. If they start going stale, a short blast in the microwave brings the crispness back. Sun-dried banana has higher moisture, so keeping it in the fridge makes it last longer and stops mould.
